No more lost aircraft

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
...new technology to prevent aircraft from becoming lost

Unique Selling Point:
New technology developed in South Africa that will impact aviation globally.

Summary:
We all think aircraft are tracked with precision throughout the flight. It is not the case! On long haul flights over Africa and oceans, flights disappear from radar and tracking apps. The only way airlines know where their planes are, is to let the aircraft send their locations via radio every hour. If the electrical system on the plane packs up or if the device is switched off as in the Malaysia plane, nobody knows where the plane is. New technology developed in South Africa now offers a way to track planes so that they will never again get lost. It is something that will impact aviation globally.

Further information:
No More Lost Aircraft
Air disasters where aircraft go missing like Malaysian Airlines Flight 370, the Egypt Air flight 804 and Air France flight 447 have alerted the international aviation fraternity to the huge problems associated with long distance flying. In anything goes wrong, there is currently no way to detect it remotely and because there are no systems in place, it makes it almost impossible find the exact location of a crash/disaster.

We all think aircraft are tracked with precision throughout the flight. It is not the case! On long haul flights over Africa and oceans, flights disappear from radar and tracking apps. The only way airlines know where their planes are, is to let the aircraft send their locations via radio every hour. If the electrical system on the plane packs up or if the device is switched off as in the Malaysia plane, nobody knows where the plane is.

After the MH370 disaster, planes now send locations out every 30 minutes. This is good, but if anything goes wrong, this practice still results in a search area of about 650 000 square kilometres – half the size of South Africa. This is because a plane flies at 900 km per hour.

There is currently no system that can monitor a plane with precision its entire route.

But this is about to change. A South African company has developed technology to do live in-air credit card transactions. This has so far not been possible. They succeeded with their technology shortly after the MH470 disappearance and realised that their technology makes it possible to track the entire route of the plane with pinpoint precision – independent of the aircraft’s power supply and systems. If this had been on board the MH370 flight it would not have disappeared.

They have obtained international permissions and permits and have CAA approval as well in South Africa. The have already tested the system on log-haul SAA flights and it works perfectly.

The international aviation authorities have called for just such a system to be in place in 2019, but so far no technology has been developed to meet this requirement – except the South African system.

It is a funky, high tech system and can be explained with real-time tracking of air craft, etc.

It is a world first and a 100% South African developed technology.

Press Release:


Missing Planes
We all think airliners are tracked with pin-point precision throughout the flight, but that’s not quite the case. On long haul flights over oceans, airliners vanish from radar for a few hours. Pilots radio their position to the airline’s operations team every hour, making this is the only way for airlines to know where their aircraft are. Consider also that airliners fly at speeds of nearly 850km/h. This results in a very large search area in the case of a missing aircraft. But, through ingenious, locally developed technology, missing planes like Malaysian Airlines flight 370 could be a thing of the past.


Script:


V/O:
In the late afternoon of 8 March 2014, an aircraft belonging to Air Malaysia took off from Kuala Lumpur on its way to Beijing. About an hour into the flight, when it was over the South China Sea, it contacted air traffic control. Three minutes later it disappeared from all radar screens --- and was never seen or heard of again.
LINK:
It is not only flight MH370 that has vanished. Several other flights also went missing in recent years.
V/O:
In June 2009, Air France flight 447 went missing over the Atlantic Ocean. Five days later some debris and bodies were found, but it took nearly three years of searching to find the aircraft.

And on 19 May 2016, this Egypt Air jet went missing over the Mediterranean Sea en route to Cairo. It took authorities 5 days to locate it.

Paul Roux is an aviation communication and aircraft tracking expert and says current systems make it possible for planes to just vanish.
Nhlanhla:
How are aircraft currently tracked?
Paul:
Aircraft currently are tracked when ground radar is available. When we start flying in areas over the ocean, there is no ground based radar availability, then they disappear. And that was obviously the concern that was brought about by MH370.
V/O:
But what do airlines do in the absence of ground based radar?
Paul:
They then have to switch and automated system which is done by the Satcom systems.
V/O:
This automated system broadcasts the plane’s position, air speed and altitude at regular intervals. It is called the ADSB system or Automatic Dependence Surveillance Broadcast. It is also the only way to track aircraft over large parts of Africa where there is no ground based radar.

The data created by the two systems is readily available and many apps use it to track planes. This one shows all the planes flying at a specific point in time worldwide.
Paul:
This is all fair and well if nothing is wrong with the aircraft. If the aircraft has no poweror if the aircraft has no systems that are required for the automatic dependence surveillance broadcast, then they disappear.
V/O:
In air disasters, where a plane suddenly stops transmitting its location, the last position broadcast is used to start a search. But that is often of little help as planes fly at nearly a thousand kilometres per hour.

For example, if a plane fails to update its position after 40 minutes, it can be anywhere in a radius of 633 km from its last known location. This results in a search area of more than 1,2 million square kilometres – larger than the whole of South Africa.

This is why it was so difficult to find the Air France and Air Malaysia planes that went missing over the sea.
Nhlanhla:
How did the international aviation community respond to the MH370 disaster?
Paul:
The International Civil Aviation Organization which forms part of the United Nations, basically picked up on the fact that there would need to ne some serious changes brought about, and they formed a committee. The systems at the time were broadcasting every 30 to 40 minutes, and they immediately set that has to be changedcd, that has to be adjusted and brought forward with existing equipment on board down to at least every 15 minutes. And that would need to be done by 2018 which is next year.
Voice:
But in 15 minutes a plane flies roughly 240 kms.
LINK:
This would still result in search area of 180 000 square km – the size od Gauteng and Limpopo combined.
V/O:
So, more frequent location reports are clearly not the solution. The international aviation body then additionally decreed that from 2021 all commercial airplanes would have to be fitted with an additional, totally independent positioning system that would still function and broadcast data, even if the airplane’s power and systems failed.

But this is a tall order and this kind of technology takes many years to create. However, unbeknown to the world, such a system had already been developed right here in South Africa -- --- by Paul.
Paul:
Our system is an independent system. It does not rely on aircraft flight deck information input, so we don’t utilize the aircraft’s GPS, we don’t us the aircrafts speed indicator, we do not use it’s position reporting functions. We don’t do anything like that. We basically take an independent reading from our own equipment that is installed on board the aircraft and we transmit that value live to the ground, so that aircraft can be tracked anytime, anyplace, and no dependent means that we do not require aircraft power, either, currently
V/O:
In addition, Paul’s equipment has been installed on two SAA planes in a test phase. Paul took us to OR Tambo to one of the planes that is currently being used. The equipment is compact – it is basically this unit that is installed on a plane. Although Paul has developed the system only an SAA technician is allowed to actually install it. Once slotted in, it immediately starts broadcasting data via satellites. This can be picked up anywhere in the world, and Paul can even monitor the plane from any portable device.
LINK:
This position of the server is only temporary and used for the test phase. In future, it will be installed where nobody can tamper with it.
V/O:
The installation of the system on the 2 SAA planes have also been approved by the South African Civil Aviation Authority says Simon Segwabe.
Simon:
The approval was basically followed by an application that was received by a local operator, but prior to the installation the CAA conducts a due diligence to ensure that the product complies with the necessary aviation standard before installation. Then post installation there would be the necessary tests done. Only upon the successful tests, then the CAA would issue approval for such installation. The approval was issued in July 2017.
V/O:
The system has also been approved by the European Aviation Safety Agency.

Back at his office Paul showed us a flight they tracked to Hong Kong. Every few minutes a position is broadcast, showing the exact flight path.
Paul
And you will see this particular area over here has formed a solid blue line.
V/O:
And what looks like a solid blue line is actually where their system started to broadcast a position every 15 seconds because an anomaly was detected and it went into distress mode. This was caused by a storm en route and in it the plane’s altitude suddenly fluctuated like this graph shows. The system sensed the fluctuations and started to send locations every 15 seconds. When they were through the storm, the system detected that everything was stable again.
Paul:
And then went back into the state of normal transmission again as per the requirements for autonomous distress tracking.
V/O:
Currently when anything happens to a plane, investigators have to wait for the black boxes to be recovered to know what has occurred.

With Paul’s system, data is transmitted as events take place, so one can know what happened to the plane long before the black boxes are recovered.

In addition, the data generated can be fed into many applications. This is the data of the recent flight to Hong Kong which shows the exact approach of the aircraft over Kowloon.

But this technology was actually developed for something completely different.
V/O:
It was developed to enable real time credit card transactions on board aircraft which is currently not possible.

But the system became much more. by chance, the platform is exactly in line with the new specifications that the international aviation industry laid down for 2021.
LINK:
If this equipment had been on board flight 370 things would have been much, much different.
Paul:
With what we have been doing in our testing phase is that we have done over 100 000 transmissions in the last couple of months with the equipment on SAA and we picked up anomalies, we picked up change in altitude, we picked up turn and bank, we picked up altitude changes in bad weather. We believe currently that if MH370 had our system on board, we would have been able to see that aircraft or at least see where its last position was, yes.
